templates_considered: AUTH-010 endpoints_need_login: nearest access-control template; checks API login, not training. Did not fit as the requested control, and would be a misleading approximation.
CONF-010 sensitive_tables_need_login: needs tables carrying a tag; workspace tables have no tags, so it would judge nothing without a proposed tag. Did not use.
CONF-011 sensitive_fields_marked: schema attribute check; not about people or training. Did not fit.
CONF-012 confidential_tables_tagged: would propose tags, not enforce training. Did not fit.
AUTH-020 own_records_only, AUTH-030 no_self_promotion, AUTH-002 admin_endpoints_check_role: access-per-record or role checks; none reads training. Did not fit.

Recipe 'Protect health data' and 'Erase and expire personal data': matched the words customer data/patients, but both are built on tags and runtime controls, and the recipe's own 'cannot see' list includes people and training. Did not fit.

ask_parts_not_covered.part: every team member has completed security awareness training
before they are allowed to touch anything with customer data
ask_parts_not_covered.why: no check exists; people and access controls outside workspace definitions

assumptions: The customer means people working on the workspace, not end users of the API.
Customer-data tables would be customers, patients, payments, orders, invoices, clinical_notes; this was only an assumption and no policy was written from it.
confusions: The skill says to write no policy only when no part of the request is checkable, but also warns against approximations that check something else. For a request about people's training, the skill's 'What no check can see' section lists people and training, which settled it, but the step-5 rule alone would not have. A sentence in step 5 naming people-based requests would help.

Tables in this workspace carry no tags and no sensitive attributes, so the tag-based recipes (health data, personal data) would need a tagging step before they judge anything. The recipes say this, but the workspace-side precondition was not obvious when reading the request alone.
The skill has no template or recipe for 'only trained or approved people can change this data'. The closest is the CONF-010/CONF-011 family, which are about endpoints and schema rather than people.
wished_for: A short section mapping common non-technical asks (training, background checks, access reviews) to the right non-policy control, so the assistant can route the customer without guessing.
An example of an advisory policy that says in its statement what it does not cover, for when the closest checkable control is only partial.
why_confidence: High confidence that no policy can check security training or who may touch customer data: the skill's 'What no check can see' section names people and training explicitly, and no catalogue check reads them. I did not run xano policy evaluate or push because no policy file was written; no workspace changes were made. The workspace was read with xano workspace pull and xano policy list only.
